# FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D

Feng Chen    Jianguo Huang    Yushan Xiao    Yue Li    Bijun Tang   
Xuyu Dong    Xingguo Wang    Feiyang Xie    Jianhui Gu    Dongfeng Cao

###### Abstract

To accelerate materials discovery, language models must be able to
address problems at the research frontier. Yet textbook- and
examination-derived benchmarks primarily assess established knowledge,
leaving performance on frontier research problems largely untested. We
introduce FrontierMat, a benchmark of 330 problems drawn from frontier
academic and industrial research in fields including aerospace,
semiconductors, embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Every problem
is validated by leading experimentalists and industry experts in its
field. Each problem presents a real study and asks the model to infer a
withheld outcome or draw a conclusion from selected experimental
evidence. Problems are annotated by functional domain, material system
and the scale of the governing mechanism; 130 require cross-scale
reasoning. The strongest general-purpose model scores only 53.7 %, and
on matched problems, cross-scale problems score 8.7 points below
single-scale ones. Half of the problems are solved by at most one model,
and models fail chiefly by endorsing what is plausible rather than what
was observed. A domain-adaptation study with meta-weighted continued
pretraining and scale-modular self-distillation raises an open-weight
model from 36.7 % to 55.4 %, matching the strongest proprietary model,
with improvements on public materials benchmarks and no decline in
aggregate performance on general benchmarks. FrontierMat provides a
testbed for measuring progress toward language models that support
frontier materials R&D.

## 1  Introduction

![Refer to caption](2610.41162v1/FrontierMat_Leaderboard_v3_colm.png)

Figure 1: FrontierMat leaderboard of six evaluated models. Bars split
each overall score by the scale of the governing mechanism. Raw
cross-scale scores are higher because these problems are more often
single-answer;
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
compares matched problems.

Lighter airframes, faster chips, dexterous robots and viable fusion
reactors require materials advances pursued by academic laboratories and
industrial R&D teams. Language models are increasingly involved in this
work: tool-augmented models already plan and run chemical
experiments ([Boiko et al., 2023](#bib.bib14); [Bran et al.,
2024](#bib.bib15)), and their readiness for materials discovery is under
active examination ([Miret and Krishnan, 2024](#bib.bib16)). Their value
depends on addressing problems at this frontier. Such problems concern a
specific material system under particular application constraints, often
requiring researchers to connect defects and local structure to grains,
fibres and pores, and ultimately to specimen or device performance.
Answering them requires experimental evidence.

Current benchmarks provide limited evidence of this capability.
Materials benchmarks draw on examinations and textbooks (MaScQA, [Zaki
et al., 2024](#bib.bib4); MaterialBENCH, [Yoshitake and others,
2024](#bib.bib5); MatSciBench, [Zhang and others, 2025](#bib.bib6)) or
use language models to generate problems from papers, textbooks and
databases (MSQA, [Cheung et al., 2025](#bib.bib10); SciKnowEval, [Feng
et al., 2024](#bib.bib11)). Beyond materials, SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team,
2025](#bib.bib12)) screens candidate problems with model responses, and
ChemBench ([Mirza et al., 2025](#bib.bib3)) labels difficulty by expert
judgement. These benchmarks do not systematically combine problems from
active R&D with annotations of the mechanisms linking atomic structure
to component performance, a central requirement of materials design.

We introduce  FrontierMat
([Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In Contributions. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
a benchmark for evaluating language models on frontier materials R&D.
Its 330 problems follow three design principles:

- •
  Grounded in frontier research. Problems draw on academic and
  industrial research in fields including aerospace, semiconductors,
  embodied intelligence and nuclear fusion. Leading experimentalists and
  industry experts in each field validated every problem as relevant to
  their work.
- •
  Research outcomes as answers. Each problem asks for an experimental
  outcome or conclusion supported by a real study, requiring prediction
  from its setting or interpretation of evidence.
- •
  Explicit domain and scale annotations. Problems are labelled by
  functional domain, material system and the scale of the governing
  mechanism: micro, meso or macro. The 130 cross-scale problems also
  record the reasoning chain.

Evaluating seven proprietary, open-weight and domain-adapted models, we
find:

- •
  Performance remains limited. The strongest general-purpose model,
  GPT-6-Astra, scores 53.7 %
  ([Figure 1](#S1.F1 "In 1 Introduction ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
  129 problems are solved by no general-purpose model, and half are
  solved by at most one
  (§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluating Language Models ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
  §[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
- •
  Cross-scale reasoning is difficult. With answer format and
  construction channel held fixed, cross-scale problems are the hardest,
  8.7 points below single-scale problems
  (§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
- •
  Models select unsupported outcomes. 83 % of parsed, incorrect
  responses to multi-answer problems endorse an outcome the study did
  not report
  (§[5.3](#S5.SS3 "5.3 How do models fail? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

We also use FrontierMat to guide domain adaptation of Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
through continued pretraining (CPT) and supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
with two scale-aware components: CPT data weighted by its benefit to
cross-scale problems, and scale-specific modules trained by
self-distillation
(§[6](#S6 "6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
Adaptation raises its FrontierMat score from 36.7 % for the official
post-trained release to 55.4 %, matching the strongest proprietary
model, with gains at every scale and on public materials benchmarks and
no decline in mean performance on the general benchmarks evaluated.

#### Contributions.

1.  1.  FrontierMat, 330 problems from frontier materials research with
        research outcomes as answers and domain and scale annotations
        (§[3](#S3 "3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
2.  2.  An evaluation of seven models analysing where difficulty lies and
        how models err
        (§[4](#S4 "4 Evaluating Language Models ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")–[5](#S5 "5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
3.  3.  A scale-aware adaptation recipe that adds 18.7 points to an
        open-weight model and transfers to materials benchmarks
        (§[6](#S6 "6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

## 2  Related Work

#### Problem sources.

Materials benchmarks for language models primarily use educational
material or problems generated from existing text. MaScQA ([Zaki et al.,
2024](#bib.bib4)) collects 650 problems from a graduate entrance
examination, while MaterialBENCH ([Yoshitake and others,
2024](#bib.bib5)) and MatSciBench ([Zhang and others, 2025](#bib.bib6))
draw on university textbooks; MatSciBench uses a 31-subfield taxonomy.
MSQA ([Cheung et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) and SciKnowEval ([Feng et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11)) use language models to generate problems from papers,
textbooks and databases. Beyond materials, ChemBench ([Mirza et al.,
2025](#bib.bib3)) assesses chemical knowledge, reasoning and intuition,
GPQA ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib1)) collects expert-written
graduate-level questions, and SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team, 2025](#bib.bib12))
and MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024](#bib.bib2)) build harder
multi-discipline problem sets. Other benchmarks target property
prediction from composition or structure ([Dunn et al.,
2020](#bib.bib13); [Rubungo and others, 2024](#bib.bib18)), the use of
materials simulation tools ([Liu and others, 2025](#bib.bib19)) or
scientific images ([Alampara and others, 2025](#bib.bib17)).

#### Answer targets and scale.

The problem-solving benchmarks above take their answers from textbooks,
answer keys or source documents, and their tasks range from recall to
calculation, reasoning and prediction. FrontierMat centres on
experimental outcomes and conclusions from active research, asking
models to infer withheld results or interpret selected study evidence
([Table 1](#S2.T1 "In Sources of difficulty. ‣ 2 Related Work ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
Existing benchmarks organise problems by subfield or format but do not
annotate the scale of the mechanism that determines the answer.

#### Sources of difficulty.

Benchmark difficulty may reflect the level of study, expert labels
(ChemBench), tiers assigned from model behaviour (MatSciBench uses the
response lengths of six models), or model-based screening (SuperGPQA).
In FrontierMat, difficulty comes from the research problems themselves.
Following work on construct validity ([Bean et al., 2025](#bib.bib8)),
signal and noise in evaluation ([Heineman and others, 2025](#bib.bib9))
and errors in benchmark labels ([Gema et al., 2025](#bib.bib7)), we test
whether its verdicts are stable and its problems discriminate
(§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Is FrontierMat a reliable instrument? ‣ 4 Evaluating Language Models ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

#### Domain adaptation of LLMs for science.

Continued pretraining on in-domain text is an established route to
specialisation ([Gururangan et al., 2020](#bib.bib20)). In materials
science, MatSciBERT ([Gupta et al., 2022](#bib.bib21)) pretrains an
encoder on materials text and HoneyBee ([Song et al., 2023](#bib.bib22))
applies progressive instruction tuning. Continual instruction tuning can
cause catastrophic forgetting of general abilities ([Luo et al.,
2023](#bib.bib23)), and on MSQA several domain-specialised models trail
general-purpose ones ([Cheung et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)). Our recipe
builds on example reweighting by meta-gradients ([Ren et al.,
2018](#bib.bib24)), domain-mixture optimisation ([Xie et al.,
2023](#bib.bib25)), bottleneck adapters ([Houlsby et al.,
2019](#bib.bib28)) and distillation from privileged context ([Lopez-Paz
et al., 2016](#bib.bib26); [Snell et al., 2022](#bib.bib27)); organising
them by scale is our extension. It is evaluated on frontier problems
rather than textbook tasks
(§[6](#S6 "6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

## 3  The FrontierMat Benchmark

FrontierMat follows the three principles in
§[1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"):
it draws problems from frontier research, asks models to infer study
outcomes, and annotates domain and scale. We describe construction in
§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Construction ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
and coverage in
§[3.2](#S3.SS2 "3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D").

### 3.1  Construction

#### Mining frontier studies.

We worked with academic laboratories and industrial R&D teams at the
research frontier to identify problems from their recent work, including
results not yet published. We also drew on experimental studies in
specialist journals across aerospace, semiconductors, embodied
intelligence and nuclear fusion. These sources enter a common
construction pipeline: each study must provide a measured outcome or a
conclusion supported by data, with sufficient context to formulate a
problem. Experts assess its relevance to current research, rather than
publication date alone
([Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Construction and Expert Review ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

#### Writing problems.

Each problem presents a study setting and selected evidence, then asks
the model to identify a target outcome or draw a conclusion from the
evidence. Some problems require quantitative derivation rather than
prediction of an unreported measurement. All use single-answer or
multi-answer multiple-choice formats. Distractors differ from the
supported result in direction, magnitude or mechanism. Annotators with
graduate training in materials science follow shared guidelines and
record the source evidence for each answer, withholding the answer and
its evidence locator from the model
([Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Construction and Expert Review ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

#### Verification and expert review.

Verification proceeds in two stages. Two language models independently
check each problem for consistency with its source. Leading
experimentalists and industry experts then review every problem in their
field for relevance to their work, significance of the withheld outcome,
and whether distractors represent plausible mistakes by a competent
researcher. Experts familiar with the originating work review problems
drawn from partner research. Problems that failed any criterion were
revised or removed
([Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Construction and Expert Review ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
The problem set, options and answers were frozen before any model
evaluation.

### 3.2  Domain and scale

We annotate every problem by domain and scale to characterise its
scientific context and reasoning demands
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

Figure 3: Composition of all 330 problems in FrontierMat. Left: problems
by scale of the governing mechanism (inner ring) and, within each scale,
by functional domain (outer ring). Right: problems by functional domain
(inner ring) and, within each domain, by material system (outer bars;
percentages are shares within the domain).

#### Domain.

The _functional domain_ identifies the property under investigation:
_mechanical_ (strength, stiffness, fatigue, damage), _thermal_
(conduction, expansion, stability), _electrical_, _electromagnetic_
(shielding, absorption, wave control), _protective_ (resistance to
ablation, oxidation, irradiation and impact), and _multifunctional
trade-off_, which requires balancing two or more properties. The
_material system_ identifies the material class: polymer-matrix,
filler–polymer, ceramic-matrix, metal-matrix and carbon/carbon
composites, metamaterials, and others. Mechanical problems form the
largest domain (40 %). Matrix composites dominate this domain, while
filler–polymer systems dominate electromagnetic and electrical problems.

#### Scale.

Scale denotes the structural and mechanistic level that determines the
answer, rather than a strict length scale. _Micro_ concerns atoms,
lattices, defects and local structure; _meso_ concerns grains, phase
domains, fibres or particles, pores and microstructure; _macro_ concerns
specimens, devices and bulk response. A problem is _cross-scale_ when
the answer requires linking levels, for example predicting a macroscopic
property from micro- or mesostructure; we also annotate the reasoning
chain (e.g., _yarn architecture $`\rightarrow`$ load sharing
$`\rightarrow`$ structural strength_). FrontierMat contains 200
single-scale problems (88 micro, 24 meso, 88 macro) and 130 cross-scale
problems. All domain–scale combinations except meso-scale
electromagnetic problems are represented
([Figure 3](#S3.F3 "In 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
left), supporting analysis of performance across domains and scales
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
Domain distributions vary across scales: multifunctional trade-offs are
most numerous at the macro scale, and electrical problems are
predominantly cross-scale (24 of 39). Labelling rules are given in
[Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Problem Format and Labelling Rules ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D").

Full statistics appear in
[Table 5](#A1.T5 "In Appendix A Problem Format and Labelling Rules ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
([Appendix A](#A1 "Appendix A Problem Format and Labelling Rules ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
Coverage varies across functional domains and scales, so we report
results by domain and scale without claiming uniform coverage of the
field.

## 4  Evaluating Language Models

### 4.1  Setup

#### Models.

We evaluate seven models: three proprietary frontier models
(GPT-6-Astra, GPT-6-Sol and Claude Opus 5.5), three open-weight models
(DeepSeek V4 Pro, GLM-5.3 and the official post-trained
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B), and FrontierMat-Model, our domain-adapted
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B
(§[6](#S6 "6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
We enable reasoning mode where available. FrontierMat-Model and the
official Qwen3.5-35B-A3B use identical prompts, decoding settings and a
32k-token output limit; their scores average 16 samples per problem.
[Appendix C](#A3 "Appendix C Evaluation Protocol ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
gives reasoning and decoding settings.

#### Protocol and scoring.

Evaluation is closed-book: each model receives only the study setting,
candidate options and required answer format. We withhold answers,
sources and other problems, and disable tools unless stated otherwise. A
response scores 1 if its predicted option set matches the gold set, 0.5
if it is a non-empty proper subset of the gold set, and 0 if it contains
any wrong option; single-answer problems are therefore scored 1 or 0.
Unparseable outputs score 0. We report mean scores as percentages.

#### Statistics.

We report 95% confidence intervals from 10,000 bootstrap resamples of
problems and compare models using paired permutation tests. We report
differences that are not significant at $`p<0.05`$ as unresolved.

### 4.2  Main results

#### Performance on frontier problems.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

GPT-6-Astra scores 53.7 % (95% CI 48.9–58.4;
[Table 2](#S3.T2 "In Scale. ‣ 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
significantly ahead of the open-weight DeepSeek V4 Pro (47.6 %) and
GLM-5.3 (45.0 %; paired permutation test, $`p<0.01`$). GPT-6-Sol (51.4
%) does not differ significantly from GPT-6-Astra or DeepSeek V4 Pro,
nor does Claude Opus 5.5 (47.3 %) differ from either open-weight model.
Domain adaptation raises the official Qwen3.5-35B-A3B from 36.7 % to
55.4 %, the highest overall score but within the CI of GPT-6-Astra.

#### Performance across domains and scales.

No model exceeds 67.1% in any scale column of
[Table 2](#S3.T2 "In Scale. ‣ 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
and scores by functional domain range from 32.2% to 65.2%
([Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Full Results ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
FrontierMat-Model leads on both structural (57.3%) and functional
problems (53.7%). Because answer format and construction channel vary
across scales, we compare matched problems in
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D").

### 4.3  Is FrontierMat a reliable instrument?

We assess ranking stability and whether individual problems distinguish
stronger from weaker models using per-problem scores
([Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Analysis Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Rankings are stable.

Resampling the problems 10,000 times tests ranking stability among five
general-purpose models: GPT-6-Astra ranks first in 97 % of resamples,
and the two GPT-6 models remain ahead of the other three in 94 %.

#### Problems discriminate and leave headroom.

For each of the 177 problems with non-constant scores across six models,
we correlate its scores with scores on the remaining problems. 73 % have
positive correlations (median 0.36), indicating that stronger models
generally perform better on these problems. 129 problems remain unsolved
by every general-purpose model
(§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
indicating room for improvement beyond a near-ceiling benchmark (MaScQA:
94.8 % versus 94.9 % for the two Qwen models that FrontierMat separates
by 18.7 points).

## 5  What FrontierMat Reveals

Aggregate scores do not explain which research problems models find
difficult or why they fail. Using FrontierMat’s annotations and the
per-problem responses of six models
([Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Analysis Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
we ask where difficulty lies and how models fail.

### 5.1  Expert validation

The first test of a benchmark that claims to sample the frontier is
whether the people working at that frontier recognise its problems.
Every FrontierMat problem was reviewed by leading experimentalists and
industry experts in its field, who assessed whether it poses a question
their own research or development work faces, whether the withheld
outcome is the kind of result their work turns on, and whether the wrong
options are mistakes a competent colleague could make. Problems that
failed any of these tests were revised or removed
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Construction ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D");
[Appendix B](#A2 "Appendix B Construction and Expert Review ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
The problems that remain are, in the judgement of practitioners,
questions from their own work rather than exercises about it.

### 5.2  Where does the difficulty lie?

Figure 4: Where and how models fail on FrontierMat. (a) Responses to the
232 multi-answer problems. (b) Scores by scale on 202 problems with
answer format and construction channel held fixed (bars: mean of five
general-purpose models, dots: individual models). (c) Problems by the
number of general-purpose models solving them.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Cross-scale problems are the hardest.

The aggregate scores in
[Table 2](#S3.T2 "In Scale. ‣ 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
are higher for cross-scale problems (66.3% versus 45.5% for
GPT-6-Astra), but the groups differ in composition: cross-scale problems
are more often single-answer, and one construction channel contributes
only cross-scale problems. Controlling for both factors reverses this
pattern. Within the channel containing both scale types, the five
general-purpose models average 29.5 % on micro, 32.7 % on meso and 23.0
% on macro problems, but only 17.5 % on cross-scale problems among the
202 multi-answer problems
([Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")b),
lowest for 4 of five models. After weighting within-format differences
by cross-scale problem counts
([Appendix E](#A5 "Appendix E Analysis Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
the cross-scale score is 8.7 points below single-scale problems
(stratified permutation test, one-sided $`p=0.008`$), with
model-specific gaps from 4.6 points for GLM-5.3 to 11.3 for DeepSeek V4
Pro. On the same matched problems, scores are lowest for electrical
problems (19.4 %), which are mostly cross-scale because composite
conductivity depends on filler dispersion and interfaces, and
multifunctional trade-offs (19.8 %), which require balancing competing
properties. These patterns point to difficulty linking scales and
mechanisms.

#### Half of the problems are solved by at most one model.

Difficulty varies substantially across problems
([Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")c).
105 problems are answered exactly by all five general-purpose models,
while 164 (50 %) are solved by at most one of them and 129 by none, with
few problems between these extremes; on 81 of the unsolved problems at
least three models give the same wrong answer (gold in
[Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")c).
They span every scale and domain (17–56 % of each domain).

### 5.3  How do models fail?

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

#### Over-endorsement dominates.

Multi-answer problems require models to distinguish reported findings
from other plausible outcomes. Of the general-purpose models’ errors
with a parsed answer on these problems, 83 % include at least one option
the study did not support, and 49 % contain every correct option
together with at least one unsupported option
([Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")a).
Claude Opus 5.5 selects 3.03 options on average, compared with 2.33 in
the reference answer, and four of the five general-purpose models select
strict supersets of the correct answer on 35–49 % of these problems. The
corresponding rates are only 19 % for GPT-6-Astra and 5 % for
FrontierMat-Model. GPT-6-Astra instead omits correct options on 30 % of
problems. Avoiding unsupported options distinguishes the strongest
models.

#### Inferring the reported outcome.

Model explanations illustrate both response patterns
([Appendix H](#A8 "Appendix H Case-Study Problems ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
On graphene-reinforced Cu–Cr–Zr alloys, GPT-6-Astra computes the
Hall–Petch increment the study reports but declines to infer the
withheld bulk strength: “none of the proposed numerical comparisons is
established”. That contribution alone does not establish bulk strength,
making evidence sufficiency relevant to interpreting the response. On a
carbon-fibre/polyamide problem, all three proprietary models explain why
a stronger interface need not give a stronger composite, yet only
GPT-6-Sol selects the measured outcome. On Cu-doped spinel thermistors,
the model instead selects an activation-energy trend opposite to the
measured one.

## 6  Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat

#### Training.

We adapt Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (3B of 35B parameters active). _Continued
pretraining_ (CPT) uses 10.94B tokens, with a reference mixture of 78.5%
materials literature (2.13M papers on composites and two-dimensional
materials), 1.5% synthesised text and 20% general replay. _Supervised
fine-tuning_ (SFT) uses 133K instruction samples (23K
materials-specific). No FrontierMat problem, option or answer entered
training
([Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
On top of this recipe, two components target the capability
§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
found weakest: connecting evidence across scales.

#### Meta-weighted CPT.

Natural sampling is dominated by well-studied systems and single-scale
descriptions. _Meta-weighted CPT_ keeps the next-token objective but
reweights materials data by their estimated utility for held-out
cross-scale problems ([Ren et al., 2018](#bib.bib24); [Xie et al.,
2023](#bib.bib25)). Materials data are grouped into 99 buckets by
material family, scale and source. A stronger model reads a data block
as context and answers 786 probe problems written from corpus papers;
the block’s value is the gain in answer margin over a word-shuffled copy
of the same block, which controls for vocabulary and length.
Standardised bucket values set the sampling weights once before CPT,
with the token budget unchanged
([Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

#### Scale-modular self-distillation.

Evidence at different scales comes from different sources and may
conflict, so joint training lets one scale override another. After SFT,
_scale-modular self-distillation_ attaches three low-rank residual
modules ([Houlsby et al., 2019](#bib.bib28)), one each for micro, meso
and macro, to the final hidden state, and a gated fusion module combines
their outputs before the shared output head. A frozen snapshot of the
model reading the problem with the evidence of one scale teaches the
corresponding module, and the snapshot reading all evidence teaches the
fusion module ([Lopez-Paz et al., 2016](#bib.bib26); [Snell et al.,
2022](#bib.bib27)). At inference the model sees only the problem, so
each module must internalise the evidence it was taught with.

#### Results.

Adaptation raises Qwen3.5-35B-A3B on FrontierMat from 36.7 % (official
release) to 55.4 %, matching the strongest proprietary model and gaining
at every scale and domain, from 13.3 points on meso to 27.2 points on
micro problems, with 14.7 points on cross-scale problems
([Table 2](#S3.T2 "In Scale. ‣ 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
[Appendix D](#A4 "Appendix D Full Results ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

|                   |           |           |           |         |
| ----------------- | --------- | --------- | --------- | ------- |
|                   | Materials |           |           | General |
| Model             | MSQA      | MatSciB.  | MaScQA    | Know.   |
| GPT-4 (CoT)       | –         | –         | 62.0 ^(⋆) | –       |
| Gemini-2.0-Flash  | 72.9 ^(⋆) | –         | –         | –       |
| Claude-3.7-Sonnet | 70.2      | –         | –         | –       |

([Table 12](#A6.T12 "In Truncation. ‣ F.5 Transfer and General-Benchmark Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

#### Transfer and cost.

Under matched settings, adaptation improves MSQA by 8.6 points ([Cheung
et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)) and MatSciBench by 14.0 points ([Zhang and
others, 2025](#bib.bib6))
([Table 3](#S6.T3 "In Results. ‣ 6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
Our scores exceed the original MSQA paper’s best and fall 2.8 points
below MatSciBench’s best, although those results use different settings.
MaScQA scores are nearly unchanged. The six-benchmark general mean rises
from 79.0 to 79.8, despite a 2.3-point drop on one benchmark: aggregate
performance holds, with some task-level trade-offs.

|                                    |                    |                   |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------------ | ----------------- |
| Qwen3.5-0.8B                       | Held-out           | FrontierMat       |
| CPT + SFT (natural mixture)        | 35.9               | 18.0              |
| \+ meta-weighted CPT               | 39.4  (+3.5 ^(†))  | 18.3  (+0.3)      |
| \+ single-module self-distillation | 59.0               | 20.1              |
| \+ scale-modular self-distillation | 59.4  (+23.5 ^(†)) | 20.5  (+2.5 ^(†)) |

Table 4: Ablations on Qwen3.5-0.8B. Variants independently modify the
natural-mixture CPT + SFT baseline. Held-out problems (513) use exact
match and FrontierMat its standard score. Small figures are gains, and
^(†) marks $`p<0.05`$ (paired bootstrap).

#### Component ablations.

On Qwen3.5-0.8B with a 35B teacher
([Table 4](#S6.T4 "In Transfer and cost. ‣ 6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
[Section F.4](#A6.SS4 "F.4 Component Ablations at 0.8B ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")),
meta-weighted CPT improves the CPT + SFT baseline by 3.5 points on
held-out problems and 0.3 points on FrontierMat. Scale-modular
self-distillation adds 23.5 and 2.5 points, both significant, and scores
above single-module self-distillation trained on the same distilled
data.

## 7  Conclusion

Materials R&D models must be evaluated at the research frontier. On
FrontierMat, the strongest general-purpose model scores 53.7 %,
cross-scale reasoning remains difficult, and models select plausible but
unsupported outcomes. Scale-aware adaptation guided by FrontierMat
brings an open-weight model level with the strongest proprietary model
while maintaining mean performance on general benchmarks. We will extend
FrontierMat to open-ended answers and further material classes as the
frontier moves.

## Limitations

#### Size and coverage.

FrontierMat contains 330 problems. Differences of a few points between
models and estimates for small groups, such as meso-scale problems, are
therefore subject to substantial uncertainty. Application fields and
functional domains are unevenly represented, with composites
over-represented among material systems. It therefore offers an uneven
sample of frontier materials R&D. We report results by domain and scale
to make this variation explicit.

#### Reliance on source evidence.

Answers are taken from source studies and may reflect errors in the
original findings. Some reported values are read from published plots,
with the extraction resolution recorded for each problem. Language
models were used to cross-check problems against their sources, which
may favour problems that these models can readily parse.

#### Answer format.

Multiple-choice options provide information that may be unavailable in
practical R&D, and the number of correct options in multi-answer
problems is unevenly distributed.

#### Adaptation study.

The study in
§[6](#S6 "6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
evaluates adaptation on one main model, with component ablations on a
smaller model from the same family, and its literature corpus covers
mainly composites and two-dimensional materials. The findings may not
generalise to other architectures, data mixtures or material systems,
and the general-benchmark comparison in
[Table 12](#A6.T12 "In Truncation. ‣ F.5 Transfer and General-Benchmark Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
covers only six benchmarks and cannot establish performance across all
capabilities required of a general assistant.

## Ethical Considerations

#### Expert participation.

The domain experts who nominated research directions and reviewed
problems participated as research collaborators. Group identities remain
anonymous during review.

#### Data and licensing.

Problems paraphrase research settings and reproduce a small number of
reported values. Source evidence is recorded for every problem, and no
figures or text are copied. FrontierMat is intended for research
evaluation.

#### Intended use.

FrontierMat measures performance on multiple-choice problems derived
from completed studies. A high score does not certify a model for
unsupervised use in materials R&D, where incorrect predictions can lead
to costly experimental campaigns and compromise safety-critical
components.

#### Use of AI assistants.

Language models were used to cross-check problems against their sources
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Construction ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"))
and to assist with writing and editing text and code. The authors
reviewed all content and take responsibility for it.

#### Answer annotation.

- •
  The answer is a result reported by the source study: a measurement, a
  quantity computed directly from measured data, or a conclusion
  supported by the study’s data. Simulation outputs may provide context
  and are labelled as such, but cannot serve as answers to problems
  about experimental behaviour.
- •
  Values read from plots are marked as such, together with the reading
  resolution (for example, about 10 MPa for the problem in
  [Figure 2](#S1.F2 "In Contributions. ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"));
  numerical options differ by more than this resolution.
- •
  If a source’s summary statistic differs from its underlying values,
  the answer is recomputed from the values given in the prompt, and this
  decision is documented.
- •
  Quantities use SI units or, where conventional in the field, the units
  used by the source. Units are stated in the prompt.

#### Scale annotation.

The scale label identifies the structural or mechanistic level that
determines the answer, rather than the specimen size. A problem is
_micro_ if the answer depends on atoms, lattices, defects or local
chemistry; _meso_ if it depends on grains, phases, fibres or particles,
pores or their arrangement; _macro_ if it depends on the response of a
specimen, component or device treated as a continuum. A problem is
_cross-scale_ if answering it requires a mechanism linking information
in the prompt at one level to an outcome at another. This chain is
recorded as _structure at one scale $`\rightarrow`$ mechanism
$`\rightarrow`$ property at another_, for example _clamping and
temperature $`\rightarrow`$ hole-edge damage accumulation
$`\rightarrow`$ joint fatigue life_. When two labels are plausible,
annotators select the level of the mechanism that distinguishes the
correct option from the strongest distractor.

#### Functional-domain annotation.

The functional-domain label identifies the property addressed by the
problem. A problem is labelled _multifunctional trade-off_ only if
choosing the correct option requires weighing two or more properties
against each other, not merely because several properties are mentioned.

## Appendix B Construction and Expert Review

#### Literature screening.

We retrieved 25,182 journal articles published in 2022–2026. We first
screened titles and abstracts for experimental materials studies in the
four application fields, then reviewed the full texts of the 4,000
remaining articles. Of these, we retained 2,186 as sources because they
reported a specific experimental result with sufficient context to
formulate a problem.

#### Research collaboration.

13 R&D groups participated (9 academic and 4 industrial or
national-laboratory). Their identities are withheld for anonymous
review. They contributed problems grounded in their latest research,
including work not yet published, and identified research directions for
literature-based problem construction. Their work spans structural
composites, ceramic components, polymer and coating systems,
semiconductor defects, low-dimensional materials and electrocatalysts.
Across sources, eligibility depends on experimental evidence, sufficient
context and relevance to current R&D.

#### Problem writing.

Annotators followed the same guidelines across sources: state the study
setting and selected evidence, ask for a measured outcome or a
conclusion derived from that evidence, write plausible distractors, and
record the basis for the answer. When the target is a withheld
measurement, information that directly reveals it is removed. When the
target requires quantitative interpretation, the necessary measurements
are retained. Two language models checked each problem against its
source
(§[3.1](#S3.SS1 "3.1 Construction ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).

#### Expert review.

For each problem, experts received the answer, the reported result and
its location in the source, and an explanation of each option. They
marked each problem Approve, Revise or Reject and provided free-text
comments.

#### Source publication years.

Published sources span 1998–2026. Earlier studies are included for their
relevance to problems identified by the participating researchers,
rather than as evidence of recency.

## Appendix C Evaluation Protocol

#### Prompting.

Models receive each problem in the format shown in
[Appendix G](#A7 "Appendix G Example Problems ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
in English, with no few-shot examples and no tools. Single-answer
prompts end with “End with exactly: Answer: \<letter\>.”; multi-answer
prompts ask for all correct letters in alphabetical order.

#### Answer extraction and scoring.

We parse the final “Answer:” line in each response, remove duplicate
letters and sort the remaining letters. The parsed set receives 1 point
if it matches the gold set, 0.5 points if it is a non-empty proper
subset of the gold set, and 0 otherwise, including responses with an
incorrect option and empty or unparseable answers.

#### Configurations.

## Appendix E Analysis Details

### E.1  Scale analysis (§[5.2](#S5.SS2 "5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"))

All models are evaluated on the full set of 330 problems. For the
controlled scale comparison, however, all problems contributed by
partner groups are cross-scale, so that channel provides no
within-channel single-scale comparison. We therefore use the 265
problems from the channel containing both scale types. The 202
multi-answer problems within this set form the comparison in
[Figure 4](#S5.F4 "In 5.2 Where does the difficulty lie? ‣ 5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")b.
To estimate the overall scale gap, we use both answer formats within the
265-problem set: we stratify by answer format (single-answer or
multi-answer) and compute the difference in mean score between
cross-scale and single-scale problems for each model and format. The
reported gap averages these differences over formats and models,
weighted by the number of cross-scale problems in each format. We
permute scale labels within each format 5,000 times. The one-sided
$`p`$-value is the proportion of permutations yielding a gap at least as
negative as the observed gap.

### E.2  Per-problem analyses (§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Is FrontierMat a reliable instrument? ‣ 4 Evaluating Language Models ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"), §[5](#S5 "5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"))

#### Answers.

Every analysis in
§[4.3](#S4.SS3 "4.3 Is FrontierMat a reliable instrument? ‣ 4 Evaluating Language Models ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
and
§[5](#S5 "5 What FrontierMat Reveals ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
uses one answer per model and problem: the majority answer across
samples where a model was sampled more than once, and the single answer
otherwise. Scores computed from these answers therefore differ slightly
from the means in
[Table 2](#S3.T2 "In Scale. ‣ 3.2 Domain and scale ‣ 3 The FrontierMat Benchmark ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D").
The official Qwen3.5-35B-A3B is excluded from these analyses.

#### Response categories.

On a multi-answer problem with answer set $`G`$, a response $`P`$ is
_exact_ if $`P=G`$, _omits_ if $`P\subsetneq G`$, _adds_ if
$`P\supsetneq G`$, and _other_ otherwise (it both adds and omits, or is
disjoint from $`G`$). An error contains an unsupported option if
$`P\not\subseteq G`$.

#### Reliability.

For bootstrap rankings, we resample the 330 problems with replacement
10,000 times and rank the five general-purpose models by total score.
For split-half agreement, we draw 2,000 random partitions into halves of
165 problems and report the mean Kendall $`\tau`$ between their
rankings. Discrimination is the Pearson correlation, across the six
models with per-problem answers, between a model’s score on a problem
and its total score on the other problems; it is undefined, and omitted,
for the 153 problems on which all six models receive the same score.

## Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details

### F.1  CPT Corpus

#### Sources.

Materials text comes from two internal literature collections:
composites (about 2.03M records, 1.77M distinct papers after
deduplication) and two-dimensional materials (1.40M records, 0.36M
distinct papers). We add structured extractions (English and Chinese)
and one-sentence summaries generated by Qwen3-32B (0.13B tokens), each
prefixed with its source paper title and not manually checked, plus
replay data from 23 public corpora.

#### Processing.

For each paper, we use the best available text, prioritising publisher
XML (Elsevier, JATS), then PDF, then abstract. Re-parsing previously
unparsed PDFs with PyMuPDF recovered about 400K papers. Cleaning removes
reference lists, repeated headers and footers, page-number and copyright
lines, line-break hyphenation and residual XML markup. Gopher-style
heuristics on length, alphabetic ratio, duplicate lines and collapsed
spacing remove low-quality documents. Exact deduplication uses the DOI
or the normalised title and year, followed by cross-collection
MinHash-LSH (128 permutations, Jaccard threshold 0.8). A fastText
classifier (validation accuracy 0.936) labels documents as core
($`p\geq 0.8`$), adjacent ($`0.3\leq p<0.8`$) or off-domain ($`p<0.3`$).
We exclude documents outside English and Chinese, retracted papers and
papers in clinical medicine, and hold out papers published in 2026 or
later plus a random 1%. The resulting corpus has 1.58M trainable
documents and 10.60B tokens (Qwen3.5 tokenizer; 9.15B core, 0.25B
adjacent, 1.21B off-domain), of which 8.34B come from the composites
collection and 2.26B from the two-dimensional-materials collection.
Documents are concatenated and cut into 4,096-token blocks; long
documents are split, not truncated.

#### Buckets and packing.

Core and adjacent literature is grouped by document type (research
papers versus reviews, books and chapters) and by quality tier (“hi” if
the paper’s citation percentile within its publication year is at least
0.5, otherwise “mid”). Documents are ordered by a salted hash, joined
with end-of-sequence separators and cut continuously into 4,096-token
blocks, so no text is truncated; block counts define natural sampling
proportions.
[Table 9](#A6.T9 "In Buckets and packing. ‣ F.1 CPT Corpus ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
reports pool sizes and the reference corpus mixture before materials
data are reweighted.

|                                    |               |                     |
| ---------------------------------- | ------------- | ------------------- |
| Bucket                             | Pool (B tok.) | Reference share (%) |
| Papers, hi                         | 4.11          | 40.0                |
| Papers, mid                        | 5.74          | 31.1                |
| Reviews, hi                        | 0.52          | 5.0                 |
| Reviews, mid                       | 0.24          | 2.4                 |
| Synthetic (extractions, summaries) | 0.13          | 1.5                 |
| English web / encyclopaedia        | –             | 6.0 / 1.4           |
| Chinese web / encyclopaedia        | –             | 3.0 / 0.6           |
| Source code / code solutions       | –             | 3.0 / 1.0           |
| Math web / math solutions          | –             | 2.75 / 1.25         |
| STEM textbooks                     | –             | 1.0                 |

Table 9: CPT data pools and reference mixture for the 10.94B-token
budget. Materials buckets are reweighted once before CPT using the
in-context procedure below. These proportions describe the corpus
mixture, not the learned weights within materials data. Papers are _hi_
if their citation count is at or above the median for their publication
year and _mid_ otherwise (including papers without citation data);
reviews, books and chapters form the review buckets. Replay (bottom, 20%
in total) draws on FineWeb-Edu, Ultra-FineWeb, FineWiki, Wikipedia,
FineWeb2-HQ, Stack-Edu, StarCoderData, OpenCodeInstruct, CodeContests,
OpenCodeReasoning, FineMath, InfiWebMath, OpenMathReasoning,
NuminaMath-1.5, LibreTexts, Cosmopedia and Pressbooks.

#### Replay share.

In small-model ablations, removing replay caused general capabilities,
especially Chinese, mathematics and code, to deteriorate throughout
training. A 10% share was insufficient, whereas 15–25% had little effect
on held-out materials loss; we retain a 20% replay share.

### F.2  SFT Data

The final assistant turn in each sample contains either
\<think\>reasoning\</think\> followed by the answer, or the answer with
an empty reasoning block; earlier assistant turns retain only the
answer. The dataset contains 133,101 training and 690 validation samples
(304M tokens, 202M of them answer tokens); 39% use reasoning and 39% are
in Chinese.
[Table 10](#A6.T10 "In F.2 SFT Data ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
lists the composition.

|                      |         |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Part                 | Samples | Content                                                                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| General capability   | 99.9K   | mathematics, code and science reasoning (OpenThoughts3, LIMO, s1K, Codeforces-CoTs, Nemotron-Science); Chinese reasoning distillation; instruction following (Nemotron-IF, SmolTalk2); dialogue (Firefly, SmolTalk2); structured output |
| Materials tasks      | 11.0K   | extraction from papers (EN 3.6K, ZH 3.5K), summarisation 3.8K                                                                                                                                                                           |
| General supplement   | 9.9K    | constrained instructions, rewriting, summarisation, Python, long context                                                                                                                                                                |
| Materials questions  | 9.0K    | single-choice 3.2K, multi-select 4.8K, calculation 1.0K                                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Format-aligned items | 3.4K    | recomposed, true/false, numeric-variant and newly written items from an internal set disjoint from all evaluation sets                                                                                                                  |

Table 10: SFT data composition.

#### Materials questions.

Qwen3-235B-A22B-Thinking generates single-choice, multi-select and
calculation problems from corpus papers, with a true/false judgment and
supporting evidence for every option. The same model then answers each
problem without the paper. If its answer differs from the gold answer,
it reviews the problem with the paper; problems whose gold answer
remains unconfirmed are discarded. Reasoning samples are obtained by
rejection sampling, retaining a closed-book chain of thought only if its
final answer exactly matches the gold answer; non-reasoning samples are
expert-style explanations that assess each option and end with the
answer letters.

### F.3  Scale-Aware Training

#### Meta-weighted CPT.

The objective is to favour materials data that improve performance on
held-out cross-scale problems. A direct implementation would evaluate
candidate bucket weights through virtual parameter updates and
differentiate the cross-scale loss through those updates. We instead
estimate data utility offline using a stronger model, then hold the
resulting sampling weights fixed throughout CPT.

#### In-context approximation.

We use in-context learning as a proxy for the benefit of training on a
data block, scoring buckets once before CPT. A stronger model reads a
data block $`d`$ as reference material and answers each probe problem
$`j`$; its margin $`\Delta_{j}`$ is the log-probability of the correct
answer minus that of the strongest distractor. The value of $`d`$ is

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
v(d)=\tfrac{1}{J}\textstyle\sum_{j}\big[\Delta_{j}(d)-\Delta_{j}(\tilde{d})\big],
``` |  |

where $`\tilde{d}`$ is $`d`$ with its words shuffled, providing a
control with the same words and length but disrupted structure. The 786
probe problems are written from corpus papers with a domain mix matching
FrontierMat’s and contain no FrontierMat problem. Materials data are
grouped into 99 buckets by material family, scale and source; $`z_{b}`$
is the standardised mean value of bucket $`b`$, and materials data are
resampled with $`p_{b}\propto p_{b}^{\text{nat}}\exp(\lambda z_{b})`$
($`\lambda=3`$), leaving the other data and the token budget unchanged.

#### Scale-modular self-distillation.

Let $`h_{t}`$ be the final hidden state for the problem $`x`$ and answer
prefix $`y_{<t}`$. Each scale module $`A_{k}`$, $`k\in\{\mu,m,M\}`$, is
a low-rank residual bottleneck, $`z_{k}=h_{t}+A_{k}(h_{t})`$; the fusion
module computes gates from $`[h_{t};z_{\mu};z_{m};z_{M}]`$ and returns
$`\tilde{h}_{t}=h_{t}+\sum_{k}g_{k}\,(z_{k}-h_{t})`$, which the shared
output head maps to the next-token distribution. Let
$`p_{\bar{\theta}}`$ be a frozen snapshot of the model and $`E_{k}`$ the
evidence for scale $`k`$. Define the teacher distributions

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle q_{k,t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=p_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,E_{k},y_{<t}),`$ |  |
|  | $`\displaystyle q_{\mathrm{all},t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=p_{\bar{\theta}}(\cdot\mid x,E_{\mu},E_{m},E_{M},y_{<t}).`$ |  |

The distillation loss at token $`t`$ is

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  | $`\displaystyle\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dist},t}`$ | $`\displaystyle=\sum_{k}\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{k,t}\,\|\,p(\cdot\mid z_{k})\big)`$ |  |
|  |  | $`\displaystyle+\mathrm{KL}\big(q_{\mathrm{all},t}\,\|\,p(\cdot\mid\tilde{h}_{t})\big).`$ |  |

Training minimises this loss together with cross-entropy on the
reference answer. Micro evidence describes defects, dislocations and
interaction mechanisms; meso evidence describes grains, precipitates,
fibre architecture, porosity and phase distribution; macro evidence
summarises property curves and test and service conditions.

### F.4  Component Ablations at 0.8B

#### Setup.

For the CPT comparison in
[Table 4](#S6.T4 "In Transfer and cost. ‣ 6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D"),
we train Qwen3.5-0.8B with the same 1.2B-token budget and SFT procedure,
using either natural sampling proportions or the in-context bucket
weights above. Distillation variants start from the natural-mixture
CPT + SFT model. *Scale-modular self-distillation* is implemented with
low-rank adapters on the frozen SFT model. Because a 0.8B model reads
long evidence unreliably, the evidence-reading teacher in this ablation
is a 35B model rather than a snapshot of the student; it answers 1,044
training problems with evidence of one scale, or with all scales plus
the cross-scale causal statements reported by the authors, extracted
from about 1,600 source papers, and only correct responses, including
their reasoning, are kept as targets. A shared adapter trained on all
distilled data is merged first; three scale adapters (rank 16) are then
trained on the data of their scale, and a per-layer gate over them plus
a fusion adapter on the all-evidence data. The *single-module
self-distillation* baseline trains a single rank-64 adapter on exactly
the same distilled data.

#### Evaluation.

Reasoning is enabled with temperature 0.6. Held-out problems are
generated as in
[Appendix F](#A6 "Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
from papers excluded from all training, sampled four times with up to
12k output tokens and scored by exact match. FrontierMat is sampled
eight times with up to 32k output tokens, over three seeds for the CPT
comparison and two for the distillation comparison, and scored with its
standard rule
(§[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Setup ‣ 4 Evaluating Language Models ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")).
Differences use a paired bootstrap over problems. The two evaluations
differ in metric and output budget, so the magnitudes of their gains are
not directly comparable.
[Table 11](#A6.T11 "In Evaluation. ‣ F.4 Component Ablations at 0.8B ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
lists all differences; meta-weighted CPT also lowers the held-out CPT
materials loss from 1.8549 to 1.8529.

|  |  |  |
|----|----|----|
|  Comparison | Held-out | FrontierMat |
|  Meta-weighted vs. natural CPT | +3.5 \[1.1, 5.9\] | +0.3 \[$`-`$0.6, 1.1\] |
|  Scale-modular vs. CPT + SFT | +23.5 \[20.1, 26.9\] | +2.5 \[0.5, 4.6\] |
|  Scale-modular vs. single-module | +0.4 \[$`-`$2.0, 2.9\] | +0.4 \[$`-`$1.2, 2.0\] |

Table 11: Differences (points) in the 0.8B ablations, with 95%
paired-bootstrap intervals (held-out: exact match; FrontierMat: score).

### F.5  Transfer and General-Benchmark Evaluation

#### Truncation.

7.6 % of the official model’s responses on multi-answer problems reach
the 32k-token limit; scoring all of them as correct would add at most
7.6 points, compared with a gap of 22.2 points on those problems (16.1 %
versus 38.3 %).

Both models in
[Table 3](#S6.T3 "In Results. ‣ 6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
and
[Table 12](#A6.T12 "In Truncation. ‣ F.5 Transfer and General-Benchmark Evaluation ‣ Appendix F Domain-Adaptation Details ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D")
are evaluated with the same harness, prompts and decoding settings, with
reasoning mode enabled throughout. Materials benchmarks are scored with
each benchmark’s released protocol: the 1,757 binary questions of MSQA,
the 1,025 text-only questions of MatSciBench and all 650 questions of
MaScQA, the subsets for which the original papers report the results
quoted in
[Table 3](#S6.T3 "In Results. ‣ 6 Guiding Domain Adaptation with FrontierMat ‣ FrontierMat: Benchmarking Language Models at the Frontier of Materials R&D").
General benchmarks are run with lm-eval-harness on vLLM.

|                               |                        |                   |
|-------------------------------|------------------------|-------------------|
|                               |  Qwen3.5- 35B-A3B      | FrontierMat-Model |
| *Public materials benchmarks* |                        |                   |
| MSQA (binary)                 | 65.2                   | 73.8              |
| MatSciBench (text)            | 58.4                   | 72.4              |
| MaScQA                        | 94.8                   | 94.9              |
| *General benchmarks*          |                        |                   |
| MMLU                          | 84.8                   | 82.5              |
| C-Eval                        | 84.6                   | 85.5              |
| GSM8K                         | 84.6                   | 85.9              |
| ARC-Challenge                 | 62.5                   | 66.9              |
| WinoGrande                    | 74.6                   | 74.7              |
| PIQA                          | 83.0                   | 83.1              |
| Average (6)                   | 79.0                   | 79.8              |
````
